title: Anti-STDP
intro: Flip the STDP window and causal pairings weaken the synapse. That sounds self-defeating, but it is how a circuit learns to cancel the parts of its input it can already predict.

blocks.source:
Δw = −A₊ · exp(−Δt / τ₊)     if Δt > 0   (pre before post: depression)
Δw = +A₋ · exp( Δt / τ₋)     if Δt < 0   (post before pre: potentiation)
Δt = t_post − t_pre

blocks.text: Anti-STDP, also called anti-Hebbian STDP, is the mirror image of the classical window. It was first characterised by Bell, Han, Sugawara and Grant at synapses from parallel fibres onto Purkinje-like cells in the electrosensory lobe of the mormyrid electric fish: a parallel-fibre input that arrives shortly before the postsynaptic broad spike is depressed. Anti-Hebbian timing rules have since been reported at other synapses, including corticostriatal synapses.
The anti-STDP curve is drawn with the classical window for reference: same shape, opposite sign.
What it computes: subtracting a prediction

The electric fish emits an electric discharge and senses the field around it. Its own discharge produces a large, predictable signal at the receptors, which would swamp the small signals from prey. A corollary discharge (a copy of the motor command) reaches the electrosensory lobe through parallel fibres at fixed delays. Anti-Hebbian plasticity weakens whichever delayed inputs coincide with the cell being driven and strengthens those that precede silence. Over minutes the cell learns a negative image of the expected self-generated signal and adds it to the input, so only the unexpected part remains.

items: A Hebbian rule amplifies whatever correlates with the output: positive feedback.
An anti-Hebbian rule cancels whatever correlates with the output: negative feedback that drives the output toward zero for predictable input.
The fixed point is reached when the learned input exactly cancels the predictable part, leaving prediction errors.
With excitatory weights and hard bounds at zero, anti-STDP alone drives many weights to zero. Pair it with inhibitory synapses, or let weights take both signs.
Anti-STDP on recurrent excitation is stabilising, and is sometimes used to decorrelate a population.
It needs a separate teaching or driving input (the broad spike in the fish) that makes the neuron fire. Without one, the neuron learns to stay silent.

blocks.text: Use the same two-trace implementation as classical STDP with the signs swapped: on a postsynaptic spike subtract A₊·x_pre, on a presynaptic spike add A₋·y_post. Inhibitory plasticity that balances excitation (Vogels et al. 2011) is a related idea: inhibitory synapses grow when pre and post are coincident, which also cancels predictable excitation.

blocks.source:
if (postSpiked) w -= aPlus  * xPre;   // causal pairing weakens
if (preSpiked)  w += aMinus * yPost;  // anti-causal pairing strengthens

blocks.text: For a cortical column: predictive-coding views of cortex say that the signal worth sending onward is the part that was not predicted. Anti-Hebbian or inhibitory plasticity is one way to build that subtraction. In HTM-style column models the same job is done structurally instead: a correctly predicted minicolumn fires only its predicted cells rather than bursting, so the column's output becomes sparser and quieter when its input is expected.

Sources: Bell, Han, Sugawara & Grant (1997) Synaptic plasticity in a cerebellum-like structure depends on temporal order, Nature 387:278; Roberts & Bell (2000) Computational consequences of temporally asymmetric learning rules: II. Sensory image cancellation, J Comput Neurosci 9; Fino, Glowinski & Venance (2005) Bidirectional activity-dependent plasticity at corticostriatal synapses, J Neurosci 25:11279; Vogels, Sprekeler, Zenke, Clopath & Gerstner (2011) Inhibitory plasticity balances excitation and inhibition in sensory pathways and memory networks, Science 334:1569.
